questions.q: Why is it critical that fill probability depends on how far a quote sits from fair value, rather than being a fixed constant?
options: If fill probability were fixed regardless of quote competitiveness, inventory skewing would have no effect on anything, since the reservation price could move quotes without changing how likely either side is to get hit
Fixed fill probabilities are actually more realistic than quote-dependent ones
This only matters for the ask side, not the bid side
Fill probability should always be exactly 50% regardless of the quote
questions.explain: The entire reservation-price skewing mechanism only works if a more attractive quote is genuinely more likely to get taken -- without that link, skewing the quotes does nothing.

questions.q: What is the real verification check for whether this simulator's market-making logic is actually working?
options: max_abs_inventory staying small relative to the number of fills -- not just that the code runs without an error
Whether the code completes without throwing an exception
Whether total P&L is always positive on every single run
Whether the number of ask fills exactly equals the number of bid fills
questions.explain: Code running successfully proves nothing about whether the market-making logic is correct -- checking that inventory stays bounded is the real test that the skewing mechanism is actually doing its job.

questions.q: In the worked run, why is the total P&L ($9.22) meaningfully smaller than a naive estimate of 415 fills times the full half-spread (~$12.45)?
options: Some fills happened while the reservation price was skewed away from fair value to manage inventory, trading some theoretical per-trade edge for keeping risk under control
This indicates a bug in the simulation that should be fixed
The naive estimate is always exactly correct and the simulator's result is wrong
Fill probability has no relationship to spread capture
questions.explain: This gap is the real, quantifiable cost of inventory management -- skewing trades off some theoretical edge per trade in exchange for controlling risk, not a bug in the simulator.

questions.q: In the simulation's fill logic, what happens to inventory and cash when a buyer lifts the ask?
options: Inventory decreases by 1 and cash increases by the ask price, because the maker is selling
Inventory increases by 1 and cash decreases, because the maker is buying
Neither inventory nor cash changes when the ask is lifted
Only cash changes; inventory is unaffected by ask-side fills
questions.explain: A buyer lifting the ask means the maker is selling -- giving up inventory (-1) and receiving cash (+ask), the correct direction for that side of the trade.

questions.q: If fill_prob_ask and fill_prob_bid were replaced with a fixed constant probability (removing their dependence on ask_edge/bid_edge), what would you expect to happen to max_abs_inventory over a long run?
options: It would likely grow much larger and potentially run away unboundedly, since the reservation price's skew would no longer influence which side actually gets filled
It would stay exactly the same as the quote-dependent version
It would automatically shrink to zero
Total P&L would become undefined
questions.explain: Without fill probability responding to quote competitiveness, the skewing mechanism has no way to actually bias which side gets hit -- inventory would behave like an uncontrolled random walk instead of a mean-reverting process.
